target_customer: Consumers buying Korean and K-beauty skincare and makeup online, later retail partners such as Sephora and Ulta that stock its brands
problem: Korean beauty products were hard for overseas shoppers to discover and buy, and brands lacked a fast route to test and sell new products abroad.
business_model: Ecommerce, first themed beauty boxes sold per purchase, then an owned multi-brand incubator selling through retail partners

founders.name: Hyungseok (Dino) Ha
founders.background_notes: Listed as sole founder on the YC page https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/mbx. Education and prior employers not found in a source opened.

competitors.name: Birchbox
competitors.what: Monthly subscription boxes of sample-size beauty products, the reference model Memebox was compared against
competitors.traction_then: More than 400,000 subscribers per a secondary account of 2011 to 2014 coverage; not verified from the dated article

technical_complexity.rationale: A storefront plus sourcing and shipping from Korea; the hard part was operations and curation, not software.

defensibility.rationale: Korean supplier relationships and curation helped, but any ecommerce rival could source the same products. The later moat was owned brands and retail partnerships.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Retailers did not buy it. Sephora and Ulta became co-development partners for its brands per the YC page.

market_need_then: Rising global interest in K-beauty in 2014 and TechCrunch coverage of the Memebox box model, with a YC partner noting boxes were sold per purchase instead of by monthly subscription.

identity.logo: Wordmark, later the short MBX mark

branding.brand_signature: Portfolio of owned K-beauty brands such as Nooni, Kaja and I Dew Care

rebrands.why: Cosmetics Business reported the K-beauty incubator rebranded to MBX; the date and reason were not opened, so the year is approximate

branding.community_and_virality: Press and review coverage of the beauty boxes in 2014 (subscription blogs, Refinery29). No fan community evidence found.

brand_strength.rationale: Memebox was widely covered in 2014 to 2016 beauty press, but the company later moved to MBX and house brands. Evidence for brand pull is thin.

pivots.to: Online reseller of beauty products, per Fortune
pivots.why: Fortune says it quickly dropped the box model for reselling; exact date not given in the snippet

pivots.to: MBX brand incubator co-developing brands with retailers
pivots.why: Reported rebrand to a K-beauty incubator; reasons not read

outcome_analysis: Memebox rode the 2014 K-beauty wave, raised a reported total above 160 million dollars by December 2016, then reshaped itself into the MBX brand incubator with Sephora and Ulta partners. It remains active and was reported in 2024 to be preparing a Korean IPO and in 2026 to have raised 10 million dollars growth capital. Revenue and profitability figures were not found.
notes: Company website us.memebox.com returned HTTP 503 when fetched. TechCrunch reports a previously unannounced Series A and a total of 29.35M after the 17.5M Series B, so the Series A is roughly 11.85M by subtraction; not recorded as an amount. An aggregator dates a 12M Series A to June 2014 (unverified). A 35M Series D in January 2019 appears only in aggregators (unverified). Totals range from 160M to 225M across sources. Headquarters conflicts between San Francisco and Los Angeles.
